question_text:
Consider the following statements:
A. Zeroth law of thermodynamics gives concept of temperature
B. First law of thermodynamics gives concept of internal energy
C. In isothermal expansion of ideal gas, $$\Delta Q \neq \Delta W$$
D. Product of intensive and extensive variables is extensive
E. The ratio of any extensive variable to mass will be an extensive variable
Choose the correct combination of statements from the options given below:

explanations.title: method2
explanations.content:
A. Zeroth law gives concept of temperature
correct. it states that if two systems are each in thermal equilibrium with a third system, they are in equilibrium with each other. this allows us to define a common property called temperature.

B. First law gives concept of internal energy
correct. the first law relates heat, work and internal energy through ΔU = Q − W. this establishes internal energy as a state function of the system.

C. In isothermal expansion of ideal gas, ΔQ ≠ ΔW
wrong. in isothermal process, temperature remains constant so ΔU = 0. hence heat supplied is exactly equal to work done, so ΔQ = ΔW.

D. Product of intensive and extensive variables is extensive
correct. an intensive quantity does not depend on system size, while an extensive one does. multiplying them (like pressure × volume) gives a quantity that scales with size, so it is extensive.

E. Ratio of any extensive variable to mass is extensive
wrong. dividing an extensive quantity by mass gives a “specific” property (like density or specific heat), which does not depend on size, so it is intensive.

explanations.title: method3
explanations.content:
The Zeroth Law states that if two systems are each in thermal equilibrium with a third system, they are in thermal equilibrium with each other, i.e., the Zeroth law gives idea about the property of temperature to be measured. Hence, statement A is true.

The First Law is the mathematical relation between heat ( $\Delta \mathrm{Q}$ ), change in internal energy ( $\Delta \mathrm{U}$ ) and work done by the system ( $\Delta \mathrm{W}$ )

$$ \Delta \mathrm{Q}=\Delta \mathrm{U}+\Delta \mathrm{W} $$

This relation introduces internal energy ( $U$ ) as a state function which is based on energy conservation. Hence, statement B is true.

In an isothermal expansion of an ideal gas, temperature remains constant, so $\Delta U=0$.

From the First Law: $\Delta \mathrm{Q}=\Delta \mathrm{U}+\Delta \mathrm{W} \Rightarrow \Delta \mathrm{Q}=0+\Delta \mathrm{W} \Rightarrow \Delta \mathrm{Q}=\Delta \mathrm{W}$.

But as per statement $C$, in isothermal process $\Delta Q \neq \Delta W$, so statement $C$ is False.

Intensive variables are the properties which do not depend on size, for example temperature and pressure.

Extensive variables are the properties depend on size, for example volume.

The product of intensive and extensive property $\mathrm{P} \times \mathrm{V}$ represents work or energy, which depends with the size of the system. Therefore, the product is extensive.

When an extensive variable (like volume or heat capacity) is divided by mass, it becomes a specific quantity (like specific volume or specific heat). Specific quantities are intensive because they do not depend on the total mass of the system. Statement E says it remains extensive, so it is False.

Therefore, only A, B, and D are correct. Hence, the correct option is (C).

question_text: An electron of mass $$m$$ is moving in an electric field $$\vec{E} = -2E_o \hat{i}$$ ($$E_o$$ = constant > 0), with an initial velocity $$\vec{V} = v_o \hat{i}$$ ($$v_o$$ = constant > 0). If $$\lambda_o = \frac{h}{4mv_o}$$, its de Broglie wavelength at time $$t$$ is _______. ($$e$$ = charge of electron)

explanations.title: method2
explanations.content:
Solution :

Electric field :

$$\vec E = -2E_0\hat i$$

Force on electron :

$$\vec F = q\vec E$$

Since charge of electron is :

$$q = -e$$

Therefore,

$$\vec F = (-e)(-2E_0\hat i)$$

$$= 2eE_0\hat i$$

Acceleration of electron :

$$a = \frac{F}{m}$$

$$= \frac{2eE_0}{m}$$

Velocity after time \(t\) :

$$v = v_0 + at$$

$$= v_0 + \frac{2eE_0t}{m}$$

de Broglie wavelength :

$$\lambda = \frac{h}{mv}$$

$$= \frac{h}{m\left(v_0+\frac{2eE_0t}{m}\right)}$$

$$= \frac{h}{mv_0+2eE_0t}$$

Given,

$$\lambda_0 = \frac{h}{4mv_0}$$

Therefore,

$$h = 4mv_0\lambda_0$$

Substituting :

$$\lambda=\frac{4mv_0\lambda_0}{mv_0+2eE_0t}$$

$$=\frac{4\lambda_0}{1+\frac{2eE_0t}{mv_0}}$$

Final Answer :

$$\lambda = \frac{4\lambda_0}{1+\frac{2eE_0t}{mv_0}}$$

explanations.title: method3
explanations.content:
The force on an electron (charge -e) in an electric field $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}}$ is $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{F}}=-\mathrm{e} \overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}}$.

The electric field is given $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}}=-2 \mathrm{E}_0 \hat{\mathrm{i}}$,

So, the force acting on electron is,

$$ \overrightarrow{\mathrm{F}}=(-\mathrm{e})\left(-2 \mathrm{E}_0 \hat{\mathrm{i}}\right)=2 \mathrm{eE}_0 \hat{\mathrm{i}} $$

Using Newton's second law of motion, $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{F}}=\mathrm{ma} \overrightarrow{\mathrm{a}}$ the acceleration of electron is;

$$ \overrightarrow{\mathrm{a}}=\frac{\overrightarrow{\mathrm{F}}}{\mathrm{~m}}=\frac{2 \mathrm{eE}_0}{\mathrm{~m}} \hat{\mathrm{i}} $$

Using the first equation of motion ( $\vec{v}=\vec{u}+\vec{a} t$ ), the final velocity of electron at any time $t$ is;

$$ \overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}(\mathrm{t})=\mathrm{v}_0+\left(\frac{2 \mathrm{eE}_0}{\mathrm{~m}}\right) \mathrm{t} $$

$$\Rightarrow $$ $$ \overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}(\mathrm{t})=\mathrm{v}_0\left(1+\frac{2 \mathrm{eE}_0 \mathrm{t}}{\mathrm{mv}_0}\right) $$

The de Broglie wavelength is $\lambda=\frac{\mathrm{h}}{\mathrm{p}}=\frac{\mathrm{h}}{\mathrm{mv}}$.

Substituting the velocity:

$$ \lambda_t=\frac{h}{m v_0\left(1+\frac{2 e E_0 t}{m v_0}\right)} $$

It is given that $\lambda_0=\frac{\mathrm{h}}{4 \mathrm{mv}_0} \Rightarrow \frac{\mathrm{~h}}{\mathrm{mv}_0}=4 \lambda_0$.

$$ \lambda_t=\frac{4 \lambda_0}{1+\frac{2 \mathrm{eE}_0 t}{\mathrm{mv}_0}} $$

Therefore, the correct option is (C).

question_text: In the hydrogen atom, the electron makes a transition from the higher orbit ($$i$$) to a lower orbit ($$f$$). The ratio of the radius of the orbits is given by $$r_i : r_f = 16 : 4$$. The wavelength of photon emitted due to this transition is _______ nm. (Given Rydberg constant = $$1.0973 \times 10^7$$ /m)

explanations.title: method2
explanations.content:
For hydrogen atom:

$$radius\ r_n\propto n^2$$

given:

$$r_i:r_f=16:4=4:1$$

so:

$$n_i^2:n_f^2=4:1\Rightarrow n_i:n_f=2:1$$

 choose quantum numbers

Since electron moves from higher to lower orbit:

nᵢ > n_f

Smallest integers satisfying ratio 2:1 are:

$$n_i​=4,n_f​=2$$

use Rydberg formula:

$$\frac{1}{\lambda}=R\left(\frac{1}{n_f^2}-\frac{1}{n_i^2}\right)$$

$$=1.0973\times10^7\left(\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{16}\right)$$

$$=1.0973\times10^7\cdot\frac{3}{16}\approx2.057\times10^6$$

$$lambda=\frac{1}{2.057\times10^6}\approx4.86\times10^{-7}m$$ 

=486 nm

explanations.title: method3
explanations.content:
The radius of an electron in the $\mathrm{n}^{\text {th }}$ orbit of a hydrogen atom is given by the formula:

$$ r_n=\left(\frac{\epsilon_0 h^2}{\pi m e^2}\right) n^2 \Rightarrow r_n \propto n^2 $$

The ratio of radii of $i^{\text {th }}$ orbit to $f^{\text {th }}$ orbit is $r_i: r_f=16: 4$,

$$ \frac{\mathrm{n}_{\mathrm{i}}^2}{\mathrm{n}_{\mathrm{f}}^2}=\frac{16}{4}=4 $$

$$\Rightarrow $$ $$ \frac{\mathrm{n}_{\mathrm{i}}}{\mathrm{n}_{\mathrm{f}}}=2 \Rightarrow \mathrm{n}_{\mathrm{i}}=2 \mathrm{n}_{\mathrm{f}} $$

For a transition to a lower orbit in a hydrogen atom, the simplest integers satisfying this are $\mathrm{n}_{\mathrm{f}}=2$ and $\mathrm{n}_{\mathrm{i}}=$ 4.

The wavelength of the emitted photon is given by the Rydberg formula:

$$ \frac{1}{\lambda}=\mathrm{R}\left(\frac{1}{\mathrm{n}_{\mathrm{f}}^2}-\frac{1}{\mathrm{n}_{\mathrm{i}}^2}\right) $$

Substituting the values $\mathrm{n}_{\mathrm{f}}=2$ and $\mathrm{n}_{\mathrm{i}}=4$ :

$$ \frac{1}{\lambda}=\mathrm{R}\left(\frac{1}{2^2}-\frac{1}{4^2}\right)=\mathrm{R}\left(\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{16}\right) $$

$$\Rightarrow $$ $\frac{1}{\lambda}=\mathrm{R}\left(\frac{4-1}{16}\right)=\frac{3 \mathrm{R}}{16}$

$$\Rightarrow $$ $$ \lambda=\frac{16}{3 R} $$

Putting the value of Rydberg's constant $\mathrm{R}=1.0973 \times 10^7 \mathrm{~m}^{-1}$

$$ \lambda=\frac{16}{3 \times 1.0973 \times 10^7} \approx 4.86 \times 10^{-7} \mathrm{~m}=486 \times 10^{-9} \mathrm{~m} $$

$$\Rightarrow $$ $$ \lambda=486 \mathrm{~nm} $$

Therefore, the wavelength of photon emitted due to this transition is 486 nm .

Hence, the correct option is (C).

question_text: A displacement current of 4.0 A can be set up in the space between two parallel plates of 6 $$\mu$$F capacitor. The rate of change of potential difference across the plates of the capacitor is nearly $$\alpha \times 10^6$$ V/s. The value of $$\alpha$$ is _______.

explanations.content:
start with Q = C V

differentiating with respect to time:
dQ/dt = C dV/dt

since dQ/dt = I, we get:
I = C dV/dt

given:

I = 4 A
C = 6 μF = 6 × 10⁻⁶ F

$$\frac{dV}{dt}=\frac{I}{C}=\frac{4}{6\times10^{-6}}=\frac{2}{3}\times10^6$$

$$\approx0.67\times10^6\text{ V/s}$$

explanations.title: method3
explanations.content:
According to Maxwell's law, the displacement current in a capacitor is equal to the rate of change of charge on the plates $\left(\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{d}}=\frac{\mathrm{d} \mathrm{Q}}{\mathrm{dt}}\right)$.

The charge ( $Q$ ) on a capacitor of capacitance ( $C$ ), connected to potential difference (V) is:

$$ Q=C V $$

On differentiating both sides with respect to time $(t)$ :

$$ \frac{d Q}{d t}=C \frac{d V}{d t} $$

Since displacement current is $I_d=\frac{d Q}{d t}$, we have:

$$ I_d=C \frac{d V}{d t} $$

The displacement current is given as $\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{d}}=4.0 \mathrm{~A}$ and the capacitance of capacitor is $\mathrm{C}=6 \mu \mathrm{~F}=6 \times 10^{-6} \mathrm{~F}$ : Putting the values,

$$ \frac{\mathrm{dV}}{\mathrm{dt}}=\frac{\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{d}}}{\mathrm{C}} $$

$$\Rightarrow $$ $\frac{d V}{d t}=\frac{4.0}{6 \times 10^{-6}}$

$$\Rightarrow $$ $\frac{\mathrm{dV}}{\mathrm{dt}}=\frac{2}{3} \times 10^6 \approx 0.67 \times 10^6 \frac{\mathrm{~V}}{\mathrm{~s}}=\alpha \times 10^6 \frac{\mathrm{~V}}{\mathrm{~s}}$

$$ \Rightarrow \alpha=0.67 $$

Therefore, the correct option is (B).

The total internal resistance is,

And the total external resistance between A and B is $\mathrm{R}_{\text {total }}=(3+3+3) \Omega=9 \Omega$

$i=\frac{E_{\text {total }}}{R_{\text {net }}}=\frac{15}{(3+9)}=\frac{15}{12} A=$ 1.25 A

Thus, the correct option is (B).

question_text: In Young's double slit experiment, the fringe width of the interference pattern produced on the screen is 2.4 $$\mu$$m. If the experiment is carried out in another medium having refractive index 1.2, the fringe width will be _______ $$\mu$$m.

explanations.title: method2

fringe width β = λD / d

in a medium of refractive index n, wavelength becomes λ/n

so new fringe width:

$$β'=(λ/n)D/d=β/n$$

given:

$$β=2.4μm$$
$$n=1.2$$

$$β′=\frac{2.4}{1.2}=2μm$$

explanations.title: method3
explanations.content:
In Young's Double Slit Experiment (YDSE), the fringe width ( $\beta$ ) is given by :

$$ \beta=\frac{\lambda D}{d} $$

Where, $\lambda$ is the wavelength of light used, D is the distance between the slits and the screen, and d is the distance between the two slits.

When the experiment is moved from air/vacuum to a medium with a refractive index $\mu$, the speed of light decreases, which in turn decreases the wavelength. The new wavelength $\lambda^{\prime}$ is:

$$ \lambda^{\prime}=\frac{\lambda}{\mu} $$

Since D and d are constant for the experimental setup, the new fringe width $\beta^{\prime}$ in the medium is :

$$ \beta^{\prime}=\frac{\lambda^{\prime} D}{d}=\frac{\left(\frac{\lambda}{\mu}\right) D}{d}=\frac{1}{\mu}\left(\frac{\lambda D}{d}\right) $$

Therefore $\beta^{\prime}=\frac{\beta}{\mu}$

The original fringe width (when setup is in air) is $\beta=2.4 \mu \mathrm{~m}$.

The refractive index of the medium is $\mu=1.2$.

Putting the values,

$$ \beta^{\prime}=\frac{2.4}{1.2}=2.0 \mu \mathrm{~m} $$

Therefore, the correct option is (B).

question_text: A ray of light passing through an equilateral prism is having velocity $$2.12 \times 10^8$$ m/s in the prism material, then the minimum angle of deviation is _______ degrees.

explanations.title: method2
explanations.content:
1. Given parameters:

Angle of an equilateral prism: $$A = 60^\circ$$
Speed of light in the prism: $$v = 2.12 \times 10^8 \text{ m/s}$$
Speed of light in vacuum: $$c = 3 \times 10^8 \text{ m/s}$$

2. Refractive index calculation:

The refractive index $$\mu$$ of the prism is given by:

$$$\mu = \frac{c}{v} = \frac{3 \times 10^8}{2.12 \times 10^8} \approx 1.414 \approx \sqrt{2}$$$

3. Minimum angle of deviation calculation:

Using the prism formula:

$$$\mu = \frac{\sin\left(\frac{A + \delta_m}{2}\right)}{\sin\left(\frac{A}{2}\right)}$$$

Substitute $$A = 60^\circ$$ and $$\mu = \sqrt{2}$$ into the formula:

$$$\sqrt{2} = \frac{\sin\left(\frac{60^\circ + \delta_m}{2}\right)}{\sin(30^\circ)}$$$

Since $$\sin(30^\circ) = \frac{1}{2}$$:

$$$\sqrt{2} \cdot \frac{1}{2} = \sin\left(\frac{60^\circ + \delta_m}{2}\right)$$$

$$$\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} = \sin\left(\frac{60^\circ + \delta_m}{2}\right)$$$

Since $$\sin(45^\circ) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$$:

$$$\frac{60^\circ + \delta_m}{2} = 45^\circ$$$

$$$60^\circ + \delta_m = 90^\circ$$$

$$$\delta_m = 30^\circ$$$

The minimum angle of deviation is 30 degrees.

explanations.title: method3
explanations.content:
The refractive index is the ratio of the speed of light in a vacuum (c) to the speed of light in the medium (v).

$$ \mu=\frac{c}{v} $$

The speed of light in vacuum is $\mathrm{c}=3 \times 10^8 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$ and the speed of light in material of prism is given as $\mathrm{v}= 2.12 \times 10^8 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$.

So, the refractive index of material of prism is;

$$ \mu=\frac{3 \times 10^8}{2.12 \times 10^8} \approx 1.414 \approx \sqrt{2} $$

As the prism is equilateral, so the angle of prism is $\mathrm{A}=60^{\circ}$.

The the angle of minimum deviation through prism is given as,

$$ \mu=\frac{\sin \left(\frac{A+\delta_m}{2}\right)}{\sin \left(\frac{A}{2}\right)} $$

Substituting the refractive index $\mu=\sqrt{2}$ and prism angle $\mathrm{A}=60^{\circ}$ :

$$ \sqrt{2}=\frac{\sin \left(\frac{60+\delta_{\mathrm{m}}}{2}\right)}{\sin \left(\frac{60}{2}\right)} $$

$$\Rightarrow $$ $\sqrt{2}=\frac{\sin \left(\frac{60+\delta_m}{2}\right)}{\sin \left(30^{\circ}\right)}$

$$\Rightarrow $$ $\sqrt{2} \times 0.5=\sin \left(\frac{60+\delta_m}{2}\right)$

$$\Rightarrow $$ $\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}=\sin \left(\frac{60+\delta_m}{2}\right) \Rightarrow \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}=\sin \left(\frac{60+\delta_m}{2}\right)=\sin 45^{\circ}$

$$\Rightarrow $$ $45^{\circ}=\frac{60+\delta_{\mathrm{m}}}{2}$

$$\Rightarrow $$ $$ 90^{\circ}=60^{\circ}+\delta_{\mathrm{m}} \Rightarrow \delta_{\mathrm{m}}=30^{\circ} $$

Therefore, the correct option is (B).

question_text: Light source having wavelength 331 nm is used to generate photo-electrons whose stopping potential is 0.2 V. The work function of the used metal in the experiment is $$\alpha \times 10^{-19}$$ J. The value of $$\alpha$$ is _______. (h = $$6.62 \times 10^{-34}$$ J s, e = $$1.6 \times 10^{-19}$$ C and c = $$3 \times 10^8$$ m/s)

explanations.title: method2
explanations.content:
Use photoelectric equation:

work function = hν − eV₀

step 1: find photon energy

$$E=\frac{hc}{\lambda}$$

$$=\frac{6.62\times10^{-34}\times3\times10^8}{331\times10^{-9}}$$

$$J=\frac{1.986\times10^{-25}}{3.31\times10^{-7}}\approx6\times10^{-19}$$

step 2: subtract stopping energy

$$eV_0=1.6\times10^{-19}\times0.2=0.32\times10^{-19}$$

step 3: work function

$$\phi=6\times10^{-19}-0.32\times10^{-19}=5.68\times10^{-19}$$

explanations.title: method3
explanations.content:
If the energy of an incident photon is $E$ then it is equal to the energy required to overcome the work function $(\phi)$ of the metal and the maximum kinetic energy ( $\mathrm{K}_{\max }$ ) to the emitted electron.

$$ \mathrm{E}=\phi+\mathrm{K}_{\max } $$

Therefore, $\phi=\mathrm{E}-\mathrm{K}_{\max }$.

Energy is given by $\mathrm{E}=\frac{\mathrm{hc}}{\lambda}$ where the Planck's constant $\mathrm{h}=6.62 \times 10^{-34} \mathrm{~J} \mathrm{~s}$, the speed of light $\mathrm{c}=3 \times 10^8 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$, and the wavelength of light is $\lambda=331 \mathrm{~nm}=331 \times 10^{-9} \mathrm{~m}$ :

Putting the values,

$$ E=\frac{\left(6.62 \times 10^{-34}\right) \times\left(3 \times 10^8\right)}{331 \times 10^{-9}} $$

$$\Rightarrow $$ $E=\frac{19.86 \times 10^{-26}}{331 \times 10^{-9}}=\frac{1986 \times 10^{-28}}{331 \times 10^{-9}}$

$$\Rightarrow $$ $$ \mathrm{E}=6 \times 10^{-19} \mathrm{~J} $$

The maximum kinetic energy is related to the stopping potential ( $\mathrm{V}_0$ ) by:

$$ \mathrm{K}_{\max }=\mathrm{e} \mathrm{~V}_0 $$

The electronic charge is $\mathrm{e}=1.6 \times 10^{-19} \mathrm{C}$ and the stopping potential is $\mathrm{V}_0=0.2 \mathrm{~V}$ :

$$ \mathrm{K}_{\max }=\left(1.6 \times 10^{-19}\right) \times 0.2=0.32 \times 10^{-19} \mathrm{~J} $$

So, the work function of metal is,

$$ \phi=\mathrm{E}-\mathrm{K}_{\max } $$

$$\Rightarrow $$ $\phi=\left(6 \times 10^{-19}\right)-\left(0.32 \times 10^{-19}\right)$

$$\Rightarrow $$ $$ \phi=5.68 \times 10^{-19} \mathrm{~J}=\alpha \times 10^{-19} \mathrm{~J} \Rightarrow \alpha=5.68 $$

Therefore, the correct option is (C).

question_text: A compound microscope is designed with two symmetric biconvex lenses. The objective lens is cut vertically, creating two identical plano-convex lenses. One of them is used in place of original objective lens. To retain same magnification keeping the object distance unchanged, the tube length has to be

explanations.title: method2
explanations.content:
Key idea: cutting a symmetric biconvex lens into two plano-convex halves doubles its focal length.

So,
new objective focal length $$f_o'=2f_o$$

For a compound microscope:

magnification $$M\propto\frac{L}{f_o}$$

To keep magnification same:

$$\frac{L'}{f_o'}=\frac{L}{f_o}$$

$$\frac{L'}{2f_o}=\frac{L}{f_o}\Rightarrow L'=2L$$

final answer:
tube length must be doubled

explanations.title: method3
explanations.content:
According to the lens maker's formula, the focal length (f) of a symmetric biconvex lens with radius of curvature R and refractive index $\mu$ is :

$$ \frac{1}{f}=(\mu-1)\left(\frac{1}{R}-\frac{1}{-R}\right)=\frac{2(\mu-1)}{R} $$

When the lens is cut vertically, the new lens is plano-convex with one flat surface ( $\mathrm{R}_2=\infty$ ). Its focal length $\left(f^{\prime}\right)$ is :

$$ \frac{1}{\mathrm{f}^{\prime}}=(\mu-1)\left(\frac{1}{\mathrm{R}}-\frac{1}{\infty}\right)=\frac{\mu-1}{\mathrm{R}} $$

Comparing the two equations, $\frac{1}{\mathrm{f}^{\prime}}=\frac{1}{2 \mathrm{f}} \Rightarrow \mathrm{f}^{\prime}=2 \mathrm{f}$, i.e., the focal length of the objective lens doubles.

The total magnification ( M ) for a compound microscope is given by:

$$ M=m_o \times m_e \approx \frac{L}{f_o} \times \frac{D}{f_e} $$

Where L is the tube length, $\mathrm{f}_{\mathrm{o}}$ is the focal length of the objective, and $\mathrm{f}_{\mathrm{e}}$ is the focal length of the eyepiece.

It is given that magnification $(M)$ and the eyepiece $\left(f_e\right)$ remain constant. To keep $M$ the same while $f_o$ becomes $2 \mathrm{f}_{\mathrm{o}}$ :

$$ M=\frac{L}{f_o}=\frac{L^{\prime}}{2 f_o} $$

$$\Rightarrow $$ $$ \mathrm{L}^{\prime}=2 \mathrm{~L} $$

Therefore, the tube length has to be increased two times to keep the magnification of compound microscope unchanged.

Hence, the correct option is (A).

question_text: Two wires as shown in the figure below, made of steel and have breaking stress of $$12 \times 10^8$$ N/m$$^2$$. Area of cross-section of upper wire is 0.008 cm$$^2$$ and of lower wire is 0.004 cm$$^2$$. The maximum mass that can be added to pan without breaking any wire is _______ kg. (take $$g = 10$$ m/s$$^2$$)

explanations.title: method2
explanations.content:
Breaking stress = $$12\times10^8N/m^2$$

Areas:
$$upper=0.008cm^2=8\times10^{-7}m^2$$
$$lower=0.004cm^2=4\times10^{-7}m^2$$

step 1: max tension each wire can bear

upper wire:

$$T_u=σA=12\times10^8\times8\times10^{-7}=960N$$

lower wire:

$$T_l=12\times10^8\times4\times10^{-7}=480N$$

step 2: tensions in wires

let mass added = mmm

lower wire carries:

$$T_l=(10+m)g=(10+m)\times10$$

=100+10m

limit:

$$100+10m\le480\Rightarrow m\le38$$

upper wire carries total mass:

$$30+10+m=40+m$$

$$T_u=(40+m)\times10=400+10m$$

limit:

$$400+10m\le960\Rightarrow m\le56$$

step 3: final

smaller limit governs → m=38

explanations.title: method3
explanations.content:
Breaking tension ( $\mathrm{T}_{\max }$ ) is the maximum tension that can wire withstand without breaking.

If the breaking stress of wire is $\sigma_{\max }$ and area of cross-section is $\mathrm{A}, \sigma_{\max }=\frac{\mathrm{T}_{\max }}{\mathrm{A}} \Rightarrow \mathrm{T}_{\max }=\sigma_{\max } \times \mathrm{A}$

For the lower wire the area of cross-section is $\mathrm{A}_{\mathrm{L}}=0.004 \mathrm{~cm}^2=4 \times 10^{-7} \mathrm{~m}^2$ :

$$ \mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{L}(\max )}=\left(12 \times 10^8\right) \times\left(4 \times 10^{-7}\right)=480 \mathrm{~N} $$

For the upper wire the area of cross-section is $A_U=0.008 \mathrm{~cm}^2=8 \times 10^{-7} \mathrm{~m}^2$ :

$$ \mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{U}(\max )}=\left(12 \times 10^8\right) \times\left(8 \times 10^{-7}\right)=960 \mathrm{~N} $$

Let M be the mass added to the pan.

As lower wire supports the pan and the 10 kg mass.

$$ T_L=(M+10) g=(M+10) \times 10 $$

For lower wire not to break:

$$10(M+10) \leq 480 \Rightarrow M+10 \leq 48 \Rightarrow M \leq 38 \mathrm{~kg}.....(ii)$$

The upper wire supports the pan, 10 kg mass, and 30 kg mass.

$$ \mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{U}}=(\mathrm{M}+10+30) \mathrm{g}=(\mathrm{M}+40) \times 10 $$

For upper wire not to break:

$$10(M+40) \leq 960 \Rightarrow M+40 \leq 96 \Rightarrow M \leq 56 \mathrm{~kg} \ldots (ii)$$

To ensure neither wire breaks, we must choose the smaller of the two values. If we add 56 kg , the lower wire will break. If we add 38 kg , both wires remain intact. Therefore, the maximum load that can be placed in pan is 38 kg .

Thus, the correct option is (B).

question_text: An a.c. source of angular frequency $$\omega$$ is connected across a resistor $$R$$ and a capacitor $$C$$ in series. The current is observed as $$I$$. Now the frequency of the source is changed to $$\omega/4$$, (keeping the voltage unchanged) the current is found to be $$I/3$$. The ratio of resistance to reactance at frequency $$\omega$$ is

explanations.title: method2
explanations.content:
For series RC circuit:

current $$I=\frac{V}{Z}$$, where

$$Z=\sqrt{R^2+X_C^2},\quad X_C=\frac{1}{\omega C}$$

At frequency ω\omegaω:

$$Z_1=\sqrt{R^2+X^2}$$

$$(where\ X=\frac{1}{\omega C}​)$$

At frequency $$\omega/4$$:

$$X'=\frac{1}{(\omega/4)C}=4X$$

$$Z_2=\sqrt{R^2+(4X)^2}=\sqrt{R^2+16X^2}$$

Given:

$$\frac{I_2}{I_1}=\frac{1/3}{1}=\frac{1}{3}\Rightarrow\frac{Z_1}{Z_2}=\frac{1}{3}$$

$$\frac{\sqrt{R^2+X^2}}{\sqrt{R^2+16X^2}}=\frac{1}{3}$$

Square:

$$\frac{R^2+X^2}{R^2+16X^2}=\frac{1}{9}$$

$$9(R^2+X^2)=R^2+16X^2$$

$$9R^2+9X^2=R^2+16X^2$$

$$8R^2=7X^2$$

$$\frac{R}{X}=\sqrt{\frac{7}{8}}$$

explanations.title: method3
explanations.content:
The impedance of a series $R C$ circuit is given by $Z=\sqrt{R^2+X_C^2}$

If the voltage of a.c. source is V then the current in the circuit is $\mathrm{I}=\frac{\mathrm{V}}{\mathrm{Z}}$

The capacitive reactance at angular frequency $\omega$ is $\mathrm{X}_{\mathrm{C}}=\frac{1}{\omega \mathrm{C}}$.

For current (I) when the frequency of the source is $\omega$.

The capacitive reactance is $\mathrm{X}_{\mathrm{C}}=\frac{1}{\omega \mathrm{C}}$

$$ I=\frac{V}{\sqrt{R^2+X_C^2}} . . (i)$$

At frequency $\omega^{\prime}=\frac{\omega}{4}$, the new reactance $\mathrm{X}_{\mathrm{C}}^{\prime}$ becomes $\mathrm{X}_{\mathrm{C}}^{\prime}=\frac{1}{(\omega / 4) \mathrm{C}}=\frac{4}{\frac{1}{\omega \mathrm{C}}}=4 \mathrm{X}_{\mathrm{C}}$

The new current $\mathrm{I}^{\prime}=\mathrm{I} / 3$ :

$$\frac{I}{3}=\frac{V}{\sqrt{R^2+\left(4 X_C\right)^2}}=\frac{V}{\sqrt{R^2+16 X_C^2}} \ldots (ii) $$

Substituting I from equation (i) into equation (ii) :

$$ \frac{1}{3}\left(\frac{V}{\sqrt{R^2+X_C^2}}\right)=\frac{V}{\sqrt{R^2+16 X_C^2}} $$

$$\Rightarrow $$ $\frac{1}{9\left(R^2+X_C^2\right)}=\frac{1}{R^2+16 X_C^2}$

$$\Rightarrow $$ $R^2+16 X_C^2=9 R^2+9 X_C^2$

$$\Rightarrow $$ $$ 7 X_C^2=8 R^2 $$

So, the ratio of resistance to reactance $\left(\frac{\mathrm{R}}{\mathrm{x}_{\mathrm{C}}}\right)$

$$ \frac{\mathrm{R}^2}{\mathrm{X}_{\mathrm{C}}^2}=\frac{7}{8} $$

$$\Rightarrow $$$$ \frac{\mathrm{R}}{\mathrm{X}_{\mathrm{C}}}=\sqrt{\frac{7}{8}} $$

Therefore, correct option is (C).

LED-2 glows when:

then A + B = 1 is already satisfied (since A = 1)

so B can be 0 or 1

final answer:

A B C Y1 = A + B Y2 = (A + B) Â· C Y3 = A Â· C

question_text: A cube has side length 5 cm and modulus of rigidity $$10^5$$ N/m$$^2$$. The displacement produced by a force of 10 N in the upper face of cube is _______ mm.

explanations.title: method2
explanations.content:
Use shear relation:

shear modulus $$G=\frac{\text{stress}}{\text{strain}}$$

$$G=\frac{F/A}{x/L}\Rightarrow x=\frac{FL}{AG}$$

given:

side = 5 cm = 0.05 m
area $$A=(0.05)2=2.5\times10^{-3}m^2$$
L=0.05m
F=10
$$G=10^5$$



$$x=\frac{10\times0.05}{2.5\times10^{-3}\times10^5}$$

$$=\frac{0.5}{250}=0.002m$$

=2 mm

explanations.title: method3
explanations.content:
The modulus of rigidity (or shear modulus) is defined as the ratio of shear stress to shear strain.

$$ \eta=\frac{\text { Shear Stress }}{\text { Shear Strain }}=\frac{\mathrm{F} / \mathrm{A}}{\Delta \mathrm{x} / \mathrm{L}} $$

Where F is the tangential force applied, A is the area of the face, $\Delta \mathrm{x}$ is the relative displacement and L is the height (side length) of the cube.

The side length of cube is $\mathrm{L}=5 \mathrm{~cm}=0.05 \mathrm{~m}$

So, the area is $\mathrm{A}=\mathrm{L}^2=(0.05)^2=0.0025 \mathrm{~m}^2=2.5 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{~m}^2$

The magnitude of applied tangential force is $\mathrm{F}=10 \mathrm{~N}$

The shear modulus is $\eta=10^5 \mathrm{~N} / \mathrm{m}^2$

Using the formula of shear modulus;

$$ \eta=\frac{\mathrm{FL}}{\mathrm{~A} \Delta \mathrm{x}} \Rightarrow \Delta \mathrm{x}=\frac{\mathrm{FL}}{\mathrm{~A} \eta} $$

Putting the values,

$\Delta \mathrm{x}=\frac{10 \times 0.05}{\left(2.5 \times 10^{-3}\right) \times 10^5}$

$$\Rightarrow $$ $\Delta x=\frac{0.5}{2.5 \times 10^2}=\frac{0.5}{250}$

$$\Rightarrow $$ $\Delta \mathrm{x}=0.002 \mathrm{~m}$

$$\Rightarrow $$ $$ \Delta \mathrm{x}=0.002 \times 1000 \mathrm{~mm}=2 \mathrm{~mm} $$

Therefore, the correct answer is 2 .

question_text: From 18 m height above the ground a ball is dropped from rest. The height above the ground at which the magnitude of velocity equal to the magnitude of acceleration (in the same set of units) due to gravity is _______ m. (Take $$g = 10$$ m/s$$^2$$ and neglect the air resistance)

explanations.title: method2
explanations.content:
For a freely falling body:

v² = 2g(h₀ − h)

Here initial height h₀ = 18 m

So:

v² = 2g(18 − h)

Given condition:

|v| = g

So:

v² = g²

equate:

g² = 2g(18 − h)

divide by g:

g = 2(18 − h)

10 = 36 − 2h

2h = 26

h = 13 m

explanations.title: method3
explanations.content:
It is given that the magnitude of velocity ( v ) must equal the magnitude of acceleration due to gravity ( g ).

$$ |\mathrm{v}|=\mathrm{g} $$

As acceleration due to gravity is $\mathrm{g}=10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^2$; so, we need to find the point where $\mathrm{v}=10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$.

Using the third equation of motion:

$$ v^2=u^2+2 g y $$

Since the ball is dropped from rest, the initial velocity $u=0$.

Putting the values,

$$ (10)^2=0+2(10) y $$

$$\Rightarrow $$ $100=20 y$

$$\Rightarrow $$ $$ \mathrm{y}=5 \mathrm{~m} $$

The ball has fallen 5 m from its starting point.

The total initial height $(\mathrm{H})$ is 18 m . The height above the ground is the total height minus the distance fallen:

$$ \mathrm{h}=\mathrm{H}-\mathrm{y} $$

$$\Rightarrow $$ $$ \mathrm{~h}=18-5=13 \mathrm{~m} $$

Therefore, at a height of 13 m the magnitude of velocity is same as acceleration due to gravity.

Thus, the correct answer is 13 .

question_text: A transverse wave on a string is described by $$y = 3\sin(36t + 0.018x + \pi/4)$$, where $$x$$, $$y$$ are in cm and $$t$$ in seconds. The least distance between the two successive crests in the wave is _______ cm. (Nearest integer) ($$\pi = 3.14$$)

explanations.title: method2
explanations.content:
Given wave:

$$y=3\sin(36t+0.018x+\pi/4)$$

Compare with standard form:

$$y=A\sin(ωt\pm kx+φ)$$

So,

k = 0.018 rad/cm

Distance between two successive crests = wavelength:

$$\lambda=\frac{2\pi}{k}$$

$$\lambda=\frac{2\times3.14}{0.018}=\frac{6.28}{0.018}$$

$$\lambda\approx348.9\text{ cm}$$

$$\lambda\approx349$$

explanations.title: method3
explanations.content:
The standard equation for a traveling wave is $\mathrm{y}=\mathrm{A} \sin (\omega \mathrm{t}+\mathrm{kx}+\phi)$, where $\omega$ is the angular frequency, k is the wave number and $\phi$ is the phase constant.

By comparing this with the given equation $\mathrm{y}=3 \sin \left(36 \mathrm{t}+0.018 \mathrm{x}+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)$, the wave number is $\mathrm{k}= 0.018 \mathrm{~cm}^{-1}$.

The distance between two successive crests (or any two successive points in the same phase) is equal to wavelength ( $\lambda$ ) of the wave.

The wave number k is related to the wavelength by the formula:

$$ k=\frac{2 \pi}{\lambda} $$

Putting the value $\mathrm{k}=0.018$ and $\pi=3.14$ into the formula :

$$ 0.018=\frac{2 \times 3.14}{\lambda} $$

$$\Rightarrow $$ $\lambda=\frac{6.28}{0.018}$

$$\Rightarrow $$ $$ \lambda \approx 349 \mathrm{~cm} $$

Therefore, the wavelength of transverse wave is 349 cm .

Thus, the correct answer is 349 .

question_text: The charged particle moving in a uniform magnetic field of $$(3\hat{i} + 2\hat{j})$$ T has an acceleration $$\left(4\hat{i} - \frac{x}{2}\hat{j}\right)$$ m/s$$^2$$. The value of $$x$$ is

explanations.title: method2
explanations.content:
In a magnetic field, acceleration is perpendicular to the magnetic field:

a ⟂ B ⇒ a · B = 0

Given:

$$B=(3i+2j)$$
$$a=(4i−\frac{x}{2}j)$$

dot product:

$$(4)(3)+\left(\frac{−x}{2}\right)(2)=0$$

12 − x = 0

x = 12

explanations.title: method3
explanations.content:
The force ( $\vec{F}$ ) acting on a particle with charge $q$ moving with velocity $\vec{v}$ in a magnetic field $\vec{B}$ is given by the Lorentz force law:

$$ \overrightarrow{\mathrm{F}}=\mathrm{q}(\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}} \times \overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}}) $$

According to Newton's second law, $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{F}}=\mathrm{m} \overrightarrow{\mathrm{a}}$.

Therefore,

$$ \mathrm{m} \overrightarrow{\mathrm{a}}=\mathrm{q}(\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}} \times \overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}}) $$

The resulting vector is always perpendicular to both $\vec{v}$ and $\vec{B}$.

Since $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{a}}$ is in the same direction as $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{F}}$, the acceleration vector $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{a}}$ must be perpendicular to the magnetic field vector $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}}$.

$$ \overrightarrow{\mathrm{a}} \perp \overrightarrow{\mathrm{~B}} $$

If two vectors are perpendicular, their dot product must be zero:

$$ \overrightarrow{\mathrm{a}} \cdot \overrightarrow{\mathrm{~B}}=0 $$

The magnetic field is given as $\vec{B}=3 \hat{\imath}+2 \hat{\jmath}$ and $\vec{a}=4 \hat{\imath}-\frac{x}{2} \hat{\jmath}$ :

question_text: In the given circuit below inductance values of $$L_1$$, $$L_2$$ and $$L_3$$ are same. The magnetic energy stored in the entire circuit is $$(U_t)$$ and that stored in the $$L_2$$ inductor is $$(U_l)$$. $$U_t / U_l$$ is _______. (Ignore the mutual inductance if any)

explanations.title: method2
explanations.content:
Let the inductance of each inductor be $$L$$ and the total current entering the circuit be $$I$$.

Since $$L_2$$ and $$L_3$$ are identical and connected in parallel, the current divides equally between them.

$$I_2=I_3=\frac{I}{2}$$

The magnetic energy stored in an inductor carrying current $$I$$ is  $$U=\frac{1}{2}LI^2$$

For $$L_1$$,  $$U_1=\frac{1}{2}LI^2$$

For $$L_2$$,  $$U_{L_2}=\frac{1}{2}L\left(\frac{I}{2}\right)^2$$

$$U_{L_2}=\frac{1}{8}LI^2$$

Similarly, for $$L_3$$,  $$U_{L_3}=\frac{1}{8}LI^2$$

Therefore, the total magnetic energy stored in the circuit is  $$U_t=U_1+U_{L_2}+U_{L_3}$$

$$U_t=\frac{1}{2}LI^2+\frac{1}{8}LI^2+\frac{1}{8}LI^2$$

$$U_t=\frac{4+1+1}{8}LI^2$$

$$U_t=\frac{3}{4}LI^2$$

Hence,  $$\frac{U_t}{U_{L_2}}=\frac{\frac{3}{4}LI^2}{\frac{1}{8}LI^2}$$

$$\frac{U_t}{U_{L_2}}=6$$

Hence, the correct answer is 6.

explanations.title: method3
explanations.content:
The magnetic energy ( $U$ ) stored in an inductor of inductance $L$ carrying a current $I$ is given by the formula:

$$ \mathrm{U}=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{LI}^2 $$

In the given circuit $\mathrm{L}_1$ in series with a parallel combination of $\mathrm{L}_2$ and $\mathrm{L}_3$.

Let the total current entering the circuit be I.

Then the current through $\mathrm{L}_1$ is $\mathrm{I}_1=\mathrm{I}$.

Since $\mathrm{L}_2$ and $\mathrm{L}_3$ are in parallel and have the same inductance $\left(\mathrm{L}_2=\mathrm{L}_3=\mathrm{L}\right)$, the current I will distribute equally between them.

So, the current through $\mathrm{L}_2$ is $\mathrm{I}_2=\frac{\mathrm{I}}{2}$ and current through $\mathrm{L}_3$ is $\mathrm{I}_3=\frac{\mathrm{I}}{2}$.

Using the energy formula for $L_2$ :

$$ \mathrm{U}_{\mathrm{l}}=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{~L}\left(\mathrm{I}_2\right)^2=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{~L}\left(\frac{\mathrm{I}}{2}\right)^2=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{~L}\left(\frac{\mathrm{I}^2}{4}\right)=\frac{\mathrm{LI}^2}{8} $$

The total energy is the sum of the energies stored in $\mathrm{L}_1, \mathrm{~L}_2$, and $\mathrm{L}_3$ :

$$ \mathrm{U}_{\mathrm{t}}=\mathrm{U}_{\mathrm{L} 1}+\mathrm{U}_{\mathrm{L} 2}+\mathrm{U}_{\mathrm{L} 3} $$

$$\Rightarrow $$ $U_t=\frac{1}{2} L I^2+\frac{1}{2} L\left(\frac{I}{2}\right)^2+\frac{1}{2} L\left(\frac{I}{2}\right)^2$

$$\Rightarrow $$ $\mathrm{U}_{\mathrm{t}}=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{LI}^2+\frac{1}{8} \mathrm{LI}^2+\frac{1}{8} \mathrm{LI}^2$

$$\Rightarrow $$ $$ \mathrm{U}_{\mathrm{t}}=\frac{4 \mathrm{LI}^2+\mathrm{LI}^2+\mathrm{LI}^2}{8}=\frac{6 \mathrm{LI}^2}{8}=\frac{3}{4} \mathrm{LI}^2 $$

So, the ratio of magnetic energy stored is $\frac{\mathrm{U}_{\mathrm{t}}}{\mathrm{U}_{\mathrm{l}}}$ is,

$$ \frac{\mathrm{U}_{\mathrm{t}}}{\mathrm{U}_{\mathrm{l}}}=\frac{\frac{3}{4} \mathrm{LI}^2}{\frac{1}{8} \mathrm{LI}^2} $$

$$\Rightarrow $$ $$ \frac{\mathrm{U}_{\mathrm{t}}}{\mathrm{U}_{\mathrm{l}}}=\frac{3}{4} \times 8=3 \times 2=6 $$

Therefore, the correct answer is 6 .

question_text: How many grams of residue is obtained by heating 2.76 g of silver carbonate? (Given: Molar mass of C, O and Ag are 12, 16 and 108 g mol$$^{-1}$$ respectively)

explanations.title: method2
explanations.content:
Silver Carbonate decomposes into Silver $$(Ag)$$ on heating:

$$Ag_2CO_3\longrightarrow\ 2Ag+CO_2+\frac{1}{2}O_2$$

The obtained residue is Silver ($$Ag$$).

Molar Mass of $$Ag_{2}CO_3$$:

$$2\left(108\right)+12+3\left(16\right)=276gmol^{-1}$$

From Reaction,

$$276g\ \ Ag_2CO_3\longrightarrow\ 216g\ Ag\ $$

therefore,

$$2.76g\ Ag_2CO_3\longrightarrow\ \frac{216}{276}\times\ 2.76=2.16g$$

Therefore, Option B is correct $$i.e$$ $$2.16g$$

explanations.title: method3
explanations.content:
$$ \mathrm{Ag_2CO_3}(s) \xrightarrow{\Delta} 2\mathrm{Ag}(s) + \mathrm{CO_2}(g) + \frac{1}{2}\mathrm{O_2}(g) $$

From the chemical equation, we can see that carbon dioxide ($ \mathrm{CO_2} $) and oxygen ($ \mathrm{O_2} $) are gases and will easily escape. The only solid residue left behind is silver ($ \mathrm{Ag} $).

Next, let us calculate the molar mass of silver carbonate ($ \mathrm{Ag_2CO_3} $) by adding the molar masses of its constituent elements:

$$ \text{Molar mass of } \mathrm{Ag_2CO_3} = (2 \times 108) + 12 + (3 \times 16) $$

$$ \text{Molar mass of } \mathrm{Ag_2CO_3} = 216 + 12 + 48 = 276 \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1} $$

Now, we can find the number of moles of silver carbonate provided in the question. The given mass is $ 2.76 \mathrm{~g} $.

$$ \text{Number of moles} = \frac{\text{Given mass}}{\text{Molar mass}} $$

$$ \text{Moles of } \mathrm{Ag_2CO_3} = \frac{2.76 \mathrm{~g}}{276 \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}} = 0.01 \mathrm{~mol} $$

Using the stoichiometry from our balanced chemical equation, we know that heating $ 1 \mathrm{~mol} $ of $ \mathrm{Ag_2CO_3} $ yields $ 2 \mathrm{~mol} $ of solid $ \mathrm{Ag} $ residue.

Therefore, if we decomposition $ 0.01 \mathrm{~mol} $ of $ \mathrm{Ag_2CO_3} $, the number of moles of silver residue produced will be:

$$ \text{Moles of residue } (\mathrm{Ag}) = 2 \times 0.01 \mathrm{~mol} = 0.02 \mathrm{~mol} $$

Finally, we convert these moles of silver back to mass in grams. We know the given molar mass of $ \mathrm{Ag} $ is $ 108 \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1} $.

$$ \text{Mass of } \mathrm{Ag} = \text{Moles of } \mathrm{Ag} \times \text{Molar mass of } \mathrm{Ag} $$

$$ \text{Mass of } \mathrm{Ag} = 0.02 \mathrm{~mol} \times 108 \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1} = 2.16 \mathrm{~g} $$

The mass of the solid residue obtained is $ 2.16 \mathrm{~g} $.

Correct Option: Option B

question_text:
Arrange the following atomic orbitals of multi electron atoms in order of increasing energy.
A. $$n = 3, l = 2, m = +1$$
B. $$n = 4, l = 0, m = 0$$
C. $$n = 6, l = 1, m = 0$$
D. $$n = 5, l = 1, m = +1$$
E. $$n = 2, l = 1, m = +1$$
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

explanations.title: method2
explanations.content:
For multi-electron atoms, the energy of an atomic orbital is determined using Bohr-Bury's $$n+l$$ rule:

  • Orbitals with a lower $$n+l$$ value have lower energy.
  • If two orbitals have the same $$n+l$$ value, the one with the lower principal quantum number $$n$$ has lower energy.

    • Let's Calculate each separately:

    A. $$n=3,\ l=2\ \left(3d\ orbital\right)\longrightarrow\ n+l=3+2=5$$

    B. $$n=4,\ l=0\ \left(4s\ orbital\right)\longrightarrow\ n+l=4+0=4$$

    C. $$n=6,\ l=1\ \left(6p\ orbital\right)\longrightarrow\ n+l=6+1=7$$

    D. $$n=5,\ l=1\ \left(5p\ orbital\right)\longrightarrow\ n+l=5+1=6$$

    E. $$n=2,\ l=1\ \left(2p\ orbital\right)\longrightarrow\ n+l=2+1=3$$

    Therefore, by rules:

    $$E<B<A<D<C$$

    Therefore, Option D is correct.

explanations.title: method3
explanations.content:
For multi-electron atoms, the energy of an orbital is decided by the $n + l$ rule.

  • The orbital with smaller value of $n+l$ has lower energy.

  • If two orbitals have the same value of $n+l$, then the orbital with smaller $n$ has lower energy.

Also, energy does not depend on $m$.

Now let us identify each orbital:

  • A: $n=3,\; l=2$

    This is $3d$

    $$n+l=3+2=5$$

  • B: $n=4,\; l=0$

    This is $4s$

    $$n+l=4+0=4$$

  • C: $n=6,\; l=1$

    This is $6p$

    $$n+l=6+1=7$$

  • D: $n=5,\; l=1$

    This is $5p$

    $$n+l=5+1=6$$

  • E: $n=2,\; l=1$

    This is $2p$

    $$n+l=2+1=3$$

Now arrange in increasing energy:

$$ 2p < 4s < 3d < 5p < 6p $$

So,

$$ \mathrm{E}<\mathrm{B}<\mathrm{A}<\mathrm{D}<\mathrm{C} $$

Hence, the correct answer is:

$$ \boxed{\text{Option D}} $$

question_text:
Identify the correct statements from the following:
A. Heisenberg uncertainty principle is applicable to electrons.
B. The size of $$2p_x$$ orbital is less than the size of $$3p_x$$ orbital.

explanations.title: method2
explanations.content:
Statement A: Heisenberg uncertainty principle is applicable to electrons.

Correct,

The Heisenberg uncertainty principle applies to microscopic particles like electrons.

Statement B: The size of $$2p_x$$ orbital is less than the size of $$3p_x$$ orbital.

Correct,

Sizes of Orbitals increases with increase in Principal Quantum Number $$(n)$$

so, 

$$3p_x>2p_x$$

Statement C: The energy of $$2s$$ orbital of $$H$$ atom is equal to the energy of $$2s$$ orbital of $$Li$$.

Incorrect,

In hydrogen-like atoms, energy depends mainly on $$n$$, but in multi-electron atoms like lithium, electron-electron interactions change orbital energies.

So, $$2s$$ of $$H$$ and $$2s$$ of $$Li$$ don't have same energy.

Statement D: The electronic configuration of Cr is [Ar] $$3d^5 4s^1$$.

Correct,

Chromium shows higher stability due to half-filled $$3d^5$$ configuration.

Therefore, Option B is correct.

explanations.title: method3
explanations.content:
Statement A

Heisenberg uncertainty principle is applicable to electrons.

This statement is correct.

According to Heisenberg uncertainty principle, it is impossible to determine simultaneously the exact position and exact momentum of a microscopic particle like an electron.

So, A is true.

Statement B

The size of $2p_x$ orbital is less than the size of $3p_x$ orbital.

This statement is correct.

As the principal quantum number $n$ increases, the size of the orbital increases.

Here,

  • $2p_x$ has $n = 2$

  • $3p_x$ has $n = 3$

Therefore, size of $3p_x$ orbital is greater than that of $2p_x$ orbital.

So, B is true.

Statement C

The energy of $2s$ orbital of H atom is equal to the energy of $2s$ orbital of Li.

This statement is incorrect.

For hydrogen atom, energy depends only on principal quantum number $n$. But for multi-electron atoms like lithium, the energy depends on both $n$ and $l$ due to shielding and penetration effects.

So, the energy of $2s$ orbital in H and Li is not equal.

Thus, C is false.

Statement D

The electronic configuration of Cr is $[\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^5\,4s^1$

This statement is correct.

Chromium is an exception to the expected configuration. Due to extra stability of half-filled $3d$ subshell, its configuration is:

$$ [\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^5\,4s^1 $$

So, D is true.

Final Answer

Correct statements are A, B and D only.

Therefore, the correct option is:

$$ \boxed{\text{Option B}} $$

question_text: $$M_3A_2$$ is a sparingly soluble salt of molar mass $$y$$ g mol$$^{-1}$$ and solubility $$x$$ g L$$^{-1}$$. The ratio of the molar concentration of the anion ($$A^{3-}$$) to the solubility product of the salt is

explanations.title: method2
explanations.content:
Step 1: Find Molar Solubility (S)

  • Given solubility $$= x { g L}^{-1}$$
  • Given molar mass $$= y{ g mol}^{-1}$$
  • Molar solubility $$S = $$ $$\frac{x}{y}molL^{-1}$$

Step 2: Determine Anion Concentration and $$K_{sp}$$

The salt $$M_{3}A_{2}$$ dissociate into ions:

$$M_3A_2\longleftrightarrow\ 3M^{2+}\left(aq\right)+2A^{3-}\left(aq\right)$$

Cation Concentration $$[M^{2+}]=3S$$

Anion Concentration $$[A^{3-}]= 2S$$

The Solubility Product is:

$$\ K_{sp}=\left[M^{2+}\right]^3\left[A^{3-}\right]^2$$

$$\ K_{sp}=(3S^3)\times\ (2S^2)$$

$$\ K_{sp}=27S^3\times\ 4S^2=108S^5$$

Step 3: Calculate the Required Ratio

Ratio $$=\frac{[A^{3-}]}{K_{sp}}=\frac{2S}{108S^5}=\frac{1}{54S^4}$$

Substitute the value of S in equation:

Ratio $$=\frac{1}{54\left(\frac{x}{y}\right)^4}=\frac{y^4}{54x^4}=\frac{1}{54}\times\ \frac{y^4}{x^4}$$

Therefore, Option A is correct

explanations.title: method3
explanations.content:
Given:

Solubility of the salt in $\text{g L}^{-1} = x$

Molar mass of the salt in $\text{g mol}^{-1} = y$

The molar solubility $S$ (in $\text{mol L}^{-1}$) is given by:

$$ S = \frac{\text{Solubility in g L}^{-1}}{\text{Molar mass}} = \frac{x}{y} $$

Now, let us write the dissociation equation for the sparingly soluble salt $\mathrm{M}_3 \mathrm{A}_2$ in water. According to the stoichiometry, one mole of the salt produces three moles of the cation and two moles of the anion.

$$ \mathrm{M}_3\mathrm{A}_2 \rightleftharpoons 3\mathrm{M}^{2+} + 2\mathrm{A}^{3-} $$

If $S$ is the molar solubility of the salt, the equilibrium concentrations of the ions will be:

Molar concentration of the cation, $[\mathrm{M}^{2+}] = 3S$

Molar concentration of the anion, $[\mathrm{A}^{3-}] = 2S$

Next, we write the expression for the solubility product constant, $K_{sp}$, which is the product of the molar concentrations of the constituent ions, each raised to the power of its stoichiometric coefficient:

$$ K_{sp} = [\mathrm{M}^{2+}]^3 [\mathrm{A}^{3-}]^2 $$

Substituting the equilibrium concentrations into the $K_{sp}$ expression:

$$ K_{sp} = (3S)^3 \cdot (2S)^2 $$

$$ K_{sp} = 27S^3 \cdot 4S^2 = 108S^5 $$

We are asked to find the ratio of the molar concentration of the anion $\left(\mathrm{A}^{3-}\right)$ to the solubility product of the salt ($K_{sp}$). Let us set up this ratio:

$$ \text{Ratio} = \frac{[\mathrm{A}^{3-}]}{K_{sp}} $$

Substitute $[\mathrm{A}^{3-}] = 2S$ and $K_{sp} = 108S^5$ into the ratio:

$$ \text{Ratio} = \frac{2S}{108S^5} $$

$$ \text{Ratio} = \frac{1}{54S^4} $$

Finally, we substitute the value of molar solubility $S = \frac{x}{y}$ back into our ratio:

$$ \text{Ratio} = \frac{1}{54 \left( \frac{x}{y} \right)^4} $$

$$ \text{Ratio} = \frac{1}{54} \cdot \frac{y^4}{x^4} $$

Therefore, the ratio of the molar concentration of the anion to the solubility product is $\frac{1}{54} \cdot \frac{y^4}{x^4}$.

Option A is the correct answer.

explanations.title: method3
explanations.content:
Mixture A:

The acid is $\mathrm{HCl}$, which furnishes 1 $\mathrm{H}^+$ ion per molecule.

$$ \text{Millimoles of } \mathrm{H}^+ = \text{Molarity} \times \text{Volume in mL} \times 1 = 0.1 \times 25 \times 1 = 2.5 \text{ mmol} $$

Since the amount of $\mathrm{OH}^-$ ions is greater than $\mathrm{H}^+$ ions ($4.0 > 2.5$), the remaining solution has an excess of $\mathrm{OH}^-$ ions. Therefore, mixture A is basic, which means its pH will be greater than 7.

Mixture B:

The acid is $\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4$, which furnishes 2 $\mathrm{H}^+$ ions per molecule.

$$ \text{Millimoles of } \mathrm{H}^+ = 0.01 \times 10 \times 2 = 0.2 \text{ mmol} $$

The base is $\mathrm{Ca}(\mathrm{OH})_2$, which furnishes 2 $\mathrm{OH}^-$ ions per molecule.

$$ \text{Millimoles of } \mathrm{OH}^- = 0.01 \times 10 \times 2 = 0.2 \text{ mmol} $$

Here, the amount of $\mathrm{H}^+$ ions exactly equals the amount of $\mathrm{OH}^-$ ions ($0.2 = 0.2$). This results in complete neutralization. Thus, mixture B is neutral, meaning its pH will be exactly equal to 7.

Mixture C:

The acid is $\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4$, furnishing 2 $\mathrm{H}^+$ ions per molecule.

$$ \text{Millimoles of } \mathrm{H}^+ = 0.1 \times 10 \times 2 = 2.0 \text{ mmol} $$

The base is $\mathrm{KOH}$, which furnishes 1 $\mathrm{OH}^-$ ion per molecule.

$$ \text{Millimoles of } \mathrm{OH}^- = 0.1 \times 10 \times 1 = 1.0 \text{ mmol} $$

Since the amount of $\mathrm{H}^+$ ions is greater than $\mathrm{OH}^-$ ions ($2.0 > 1.0$), there is an excess of $\mathrm{H}^+$ ions in the solution. Therefore, mixture C is acidic, meaning its pH will be down, specifically less than 7.

Final Conclusion:

Now, let us bring it all together and arrange them in increasing order of their pH values (from most acidic to most basic):

  • Mixture C is acidic ($\mathrm{pH} < 7$)

  • Mixture B is neutral ($\mathrm{pH} = 7$)

  • Mixture A is basic ($\mathrm{pH} > 7$)

The increasing order of their pH values is $\mathrm{C} < \mathrm{B} < \mathrm{A}$.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option C.

$$k=\frac{2.303}{t}\log \frac{\text{Initial\ pressure\ of\ A}}{\text{Pressure\ of\ A\ at\ time\ }t}$$

Substituting the expressions we derived:
$$k=\frac{2.303}{t}\log \frac{p_{i}}{2p_{i}-p_{t}}$$

$$k=\frac{1}{t}\ln \frac{p_{i}}{2p_{i}-p_{t}}$$

Hence, Option A is correct

$$ k = \frac{1}{t} \ln \frac{[\mathrm{A}]_0}{[\mathrm{A}]_t} $$

Since pressure is proportional to concentration for gases,

$$ k = \frac{1}{t} \ln \frac{p_i}{2p_i - p_t} $$

Therefore, the correct expression is

$$ \boxed{k = \frac{1}{t} \ln \frac{p_i}{2p_i - p_t}} $$

So, the correct option is:

$$ \boxed{\text{Option A}} $$

explanations.title: method2
explanations.content:
Statement I: The correct order of electronegativity of fluorine, oxygen and nitrogen is $$F > O > N$$.

Correct,

Electronegativity increases across a period in the periodic table from left to right. 

As nitrogen, oxygen, and fluorine all belong to the same period and follow this trend, fluorine is the most electronegative element, followed by oxygen, and then nitrogen (forming the exact order $$F > O > N$$.

Statement II: The oxidation state of oxygen in $$OF_2$$ is +2 and in $$Na_2O$$ is $$-2$$.

Correct,

For $$OF_2$$,

Since, fluorine is $$-1$$

$$x+\left(-1\right)\times\ 2=0$$

$$x=+2$$

For $$Na_2O$$,

Since, sodium is always $$+1$$

$$\left(+1\right)\times\ 2+x=0$$

$$x=-2$$

Therefore, Statement II is also correct.

Hence, it is Option A$$\longrightarrow\ $$ Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

explanations.content:
Statement I:

Electronegativity generally increases across a period from left to right.

For the elements nitrogen, oxygen, and fluorine in the second period, the correct order is

$$ \mathrm{F} > \mathrm{O} > \mathrm{N} $$

So, Statement I is true.

Statement II:

Let us check the oxidation state of oxygen in both compounds.

  1. In $\mathrm{OF}_2$

Fluorine is the most electronegative element, so its oxidation state is always $-1$.

Let the oxidation state of oxygen be $x$.

Then,

$$ x + 2(-1) = 0 $$

$$ x - 2 = 0 $$

$$ x = +2 $$

So, in $\mathrm{OF}_2$, oxygen has oxidation state $+2$.

  1. In $\mathrm{Na}_2\mathrm{O}$

Sodium has oxidation state $+1$.

Let the oxidation state of oxygen be $x$.

Then,

$$ 2(+1) + x = 0 $$

$$ 2 + x = 0 $$

$$ x = -2 $$

So, in $\mathrm{Na}_2\mathrm{O}$, oxygen has oxidation state $-2$.

Hence, Statement II is also true.

Therefore, the correct answer is:

$$ \boxed{\text{Option A}} $$

Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

question_text:
Correct statements from the following are:
A. Nitrogen in oxidation states from +1 to +4 disproportionates in acid medium.
B. Nitrogen has the ability to form d$$\pi$$ - p$$\pi$$ multiple bonds with itself and other elements with small size and high electronegativity.
C. N-N single bond is stronger than P-P single bond.
D. Nitrogen has highest density in its group due to small size.
E. The maximum covalency of nitrogen is four since it has only four valence orbitals for bonding.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

explanations.title: method2
explanations.content:
Detailed Breakdown of Each Statement

  • A. Nitrogen in oxidation states from +1 to +4 disproportionates in acid medium.
    Status: Correct
    In an acidic solution, nitrogen compounds with intermediate oxidation states (from +1 to +4) are unstable and typically undergo disproportionation (simultaneously oxidizing and reducing). For example, nitrous acid (+3 oxidation state) disproportionates into nitric acid (+5) and nitric oxide (+2):$$3HNO_2→HNO_3+2NO+H_2O$$
  • B. Nitrogen has the ability to form dπ-pπ multiple bonds with itself and other elements...
    Status: Incorrect
    Nitrogen belongs to the second period of the periodic table and does not possess $$d$$-orbitals. Therefore, it cannot form $$d\pi-p\pi$$ bonds. Instead, it readily forms $$p\pi-p\pi$$ multiple bonds with itself ($$N≡N$$) and other small, highly electronegative elements like Carbon and Oxygen.
  • C. $$N-N$$ single bond is stronger than $$P-P$$ single bond.
    Status: Incorrect
    The $$N-N$$ single bond is actually weaker than the $$P-P$$ single bond. Because of nitrogen's exceptionally small atomic size, the non-bonding lone pairs of electrons on adjacent nitrogen atoms experience high inter-electronic repulsion, weakening the single bond strength.
  • D. Nitrogen has highest density in its group due to small size.
    Status: Incorrect
    Density generally increases down the group in Group 15 because the increase in atomic mass outweighs the increase in atomic volume. Nitrogen is a gas at room temperature and has the lowest density in its group, whereas bismuth ($$Bi$$) has the highest.
  • E. The maximum covalency of nitrogen is four since it has only four valence orbitals for bonding.
    Status: Correct
    Nitrogen has the valence shell electronic configuration $$2s^22p^3$$. With only one $$2s$$ and three $$2p$$ orbitals available (and no vacant $$d$$-orbitals to expand its octet), it can form a maximum of four covalent bonds (e.g., as seen in $$NH4^+$$).

Summary Table

Statement Evaluation Key Reason
A Correct Intermediate oxidation states (+1 to +4) readily disproportionate.
B Incorrect Nitrogen lacks $$d$$-orbitals; it forms $$p\pi-p\pi$$ bonds instead.
C Incorrect High lone-pair repulsion makes the $$N-N$$ single bond weaker than $$P-P$$.
D Incorrect Density increases down the group; Nitrogen has the lowest density.
E Correct Only four valence orbitals ($$1s+3p$$) limit its maximum covalency to 4.

explanations.title: method3
explanations.content:
Statement A: Nitrogen in oxidation states from $+1$ to $+4$ disproportionates in acid medium.

This statement is correct. All oxidation states of nitrogen from $+1$ to $+4$ tend to undergo disproportionation reactions in an acidic solution. For example, nitrous acid, in which nitrogen is in the $+3$ oxidation state, disproportionates into nitric acid ($+5$) and nitric oxide ($+2$):

$$ 3\mathrm{HNO}_2 \rightarrow \mathrm{HNO}_3 + \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} + 2\mathrm{NO} $$

Statement B: Nitrogen has the ability to form $\mathrm{d} \pi$ - $\mathrm{p} \pi$ multiple bonds with itself and other elements with small size and high electronegativity.

This statement is incorrect. The valence shell electronic configuration of nitrogen is $2\mathrm{s}^2 2\mathrm{p}^3$. Since nitrogen belongs to the second period, it does not possess any empty d-orbitals in its valence shell. Due to the absence of d-orbitals, nitrogen can readily form $\mathrm{p} \pi$ - $\mathrm{p} \pi$ multiple bonds, but it is physically impossible for it to form $\mathrm{d} \pi$ - $\mathrm{p} \pi$ bonds.

Statement C: N-N single bond is stronger than P-P single bond.

This statement is incorrect. The single N-N bond is actually weaker than the single P-P bond. Nitrogen atoms are very small, which results in a short N-N bond length. This brings the non-bonding electron pairs (lone pairs) on the two bonded nitrogen atoms very close to each other, leading to high interelectronic repulsion that weakens the chemical bond.

Statement D: Nitrogen has highest density in its group due to small size.

This statement is incorrect. As we move down Group 15 from nitrogen to bismuth, the atomic mass increases at a greater rate than the atomic volume. As a result, density smoothly increases down the group. Nitrogen is a diatomic gas at room temperature and has the lowest density in the group, whereas bismuth is a solid and possesses the highest density.

Statement E: The maximum covalency of nitrogen is four since it has only four valence orbitals for bonding.

This statement is correct. The valence shell of nitrogen consists of only four orbitals available for bonding: one $\mathrm{s}$ orbital ($2\mathrm{s}$) and three $\mathrm{p}$ orbitals ($2\mathrm{p}_x, 2\mathrm{p}_y, 2\mathrm{p}_z$). Without any d-orbitals available to expand its octet, nitrogen is strictly restricted to a maximum covalency of four.

Through our step-by-step analysis, we have found that only statements A and E are correct.

Correct Answer:

Option D (A and E Only)

question_text:
The correct statements about metal carbonyls are
A. The metal-carbon bonds in metal carbonyls possess both $$\sigma$$ and $$\pi$$-character.
B. Due to synergic bonding interactions between metal and CO ligand, the metal-carbon bond becomes weak.
C. The metal-carbon $$\sigma$$ bond is formed by the donation of lone pair of electrons on the carbonyl carbon into a vacant orbital of metal.
D. The metal-carbon $$\pi$$ bond is formed by the donation of electrons from filled d-orbital of metal into vacant $$\pi^*$$ orbital of CO.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

explanations.title: method2
explanations.content:
Synergic effect: 

The $$\sigma\ $$-donation strengthens the $$\pi\ $$-back-donation, and the $$\pi\ $$-back-donation recursively strengthens the $$\sigma\ $$-donation. This cooperative interaction is known as a synergic effect, which, results in a stronger, highly stable metal-carbon bond.

Statement A is correct: The metal-carbon ($$M-C$$) bond in metal carbonyls exhibits a partial double-bond character because it has both $$\sigma\ $$ and $$\pi\ $$ character due to the simultaneous forward and backward electron donation.

Statement B is incorrect: The synergic bonding effect actually strengthens the metal-carbon bond while weakening the carbon-oxygen $$CO$$ bond.

Statement C is correct: The M-C $$\sigma\ $$  bond is formed through ligand-to-metal L$$\ \longrightarrow\ $$ M donation, where the lone pair of electrons on the carbonyl carbon is shared with a vacant $$d$$-orbital of the central transition metal.

Statement D is correct: The M-C $$\pi\ $$ bond is formed through metal-to-ligand M$$\ \longrightarrow\ $$ L back-donation, where electrons from a filled d-orbital of the metal shift into the empty antibonding $$\pi^*$$ orbital of the $$CO$$ ligand.

Hence, Option B $$\ \longrightarrow\ $$ A,C and D Only.

explanations.title: method3
explanations.content:
In metal carbonyls, bonding between the metal and CO ligand is explained by synergic bonding.

Statement A

The metal-carbon bond in metal carbonyls has both $\sigma$ and $\pi$ character.

This is correct.

  • CO donates a lone pair from carbon to the metal, forming a $\sigma$ bond.

  • The metal donates electron density back to CO into its vacant $\pi^*$ orbital, forming a $\pi$ bond.

So, the bond has both $\sigma$ and $\pi$ character.

Statement B

Due to synergic bonding interactions between metal and CO ligand, the metal-carbon bond becomes weak.

This is incorrect.

Synergic bonding actually strengthens the metal-carbon bond because:

  • CO donates electrons to metal by $\sigma$ donation.

  • Metal donates electrons back to CO by $\pi$ back bonding.

These two processes reinforce each other, so the MâC bond becomes stronger, not weaker.

Statement C

The metal-carbon $\sigma$ bond is formed by donation of lone pair of electrons on the carbonyl carbon into a vacant orbital of metal.

This is correct.

This is exactly the $\sigma$ donation from CO to the metal.

Statement D

The metal-carbon $\pi$ bond is formed by donation of electrons from filled $d$-orbital of metal into vacant $\pi^*$ orbital of CO.

This is correct.

This is called $\pi$ back bonding or back donation.

So the correct statements are:

$$ A,\ C,\ \text{and}\ D $$

Hence, the correct answer is:

$$ \boxed{\text{Option B}} $$

Given below are two statements:
Statement I: Each electron in $$e_g$$ orbitals destabilizes the orbitals by $$+0.6 \Delta_o$$ and each electron in the $$t_{2g}$$ orbitals stabilizes the orbitals by $$-0.4 \Delta_o$$ in an octahedral field on the basis of crystal field theory.
Statement II: All the d-orbitals of the transition metals have the same energy in their free atomic state but when a complex is formed the ligands destroy the degeneracy of these orbitals on the basis of crystal field theory.
In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below

options.A: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
options.B: Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
options.C: Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
options.D: Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct

explanations.title: method2
explanations.content:
Statement I: Each electron in $$e_g$$ orbitals destabilizes the orbitals by $$+0.6 \Delta_o$$ and each electron in the $$t_{2g}$$ orbitals stabilizes the orbitals by $$-0.4 \Delta_o$$ in an octahedral field on the basis of crystal field theory.

Correct, 

According to Crystal Field Theory (CFT), in an octahedral compound, the $$d$$ orbitals split into two halves: the lower energy $$t_2g$$ and higher energy $$e_g$$. To maintain the average energy each electron of $$t_2g$$ lowers the energy by $$-0.4 \Delta_o$$ ($$i.e$$ stabilization), while each electron in $$e_g$$ orbitals raises the energy by $$+0.6 \Delta_o$$ ($$i.e$$ destabilization).

This is the basis of Crystal Field Theory (CFT).

Representation 

$$t_{2g}=-0.4\Delta_o$$ 

$$e_g=+0.6\Delta_o$$

Statement II: All the d-orbitals of the transition metals have the same energy in their free atomic state but when a complex is formed the ligands destroy the degeneracy of these orbitals on the basis of crystal field theory.

Correct, 

In a free, isolated transition metal atom or ion, the five $$d$$ orbitals possesses same energy level $$i.e$$ they are "degenarate" . When the complex is formed the negative field of the ligands interact differently with various $$d$$ orbitals which destroys the degeneracy, which leads to splitting in the energy.

explanations.title: method3
explanations.content:
$$ \text { Statement I : } $$

In an octahedral field, the five $d$-orbitals split into two sets: lower-energy $t_{2g}$ and higher-energy $e_g$.

Each electron placed in the higher-energy $e_g$ orbitals increases (destabilizes) the energy by $+0.6\Delta_o$.

Each electron placed in the lower-energy $t_{2g}$ orbitals decreases (stabilizes) the energy by $-0.4\Delta_o$.

So, when electrons go into $e_g$, the crystal field stabilisation becomes less (energy goes up), and when electrons go into $t_{2g}$, the stabilisation becomes more (energy goes down).

Statement II : In free atomic state of transition metal, degeneracy of d-orbrital is maintained.

In the free (isolated) metal ion, all five $d$-orbitals have the same energy, so they are degenerate.

When ligands approach to form a complex, the metalâligand interactions are not the same for all $d$-orbitals.

Because of this, the five $d$-orbitals split into two sets (like $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ in octahedral complexes), and the degeneracy is removed.

question_text:
For the following Friedel Craft's alkylation reaction, which of the statements are correct?


A. Major product is n-propyl benzene.
B. iso-propyl carbocation intermediate is also generated.
C. Multiple substitution is inevitable.
D. Introducing electron-donating substituent on benzene will not produce any alkyl benzene.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

explanations.title: method2
explanations.content:
• Statement A: Major product is n-propyl benzene (Incorrect)

    When 1-chloropropane reacts with anhydrous $$\text{AlCl}_3$$, it initially forms a primary carbocation ($$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2^+$$). This primary carbocation undergoes a 1,2-hydride shift to form a more stable secondary carbocation (the isopropyl carbocation). Because the secondary carbocation is more stable, isopropylbenzene (cumene) is formed as the major product, not n-propylbenzene.

  • Statement B: iso-propyl carbocation intermediate is also generated (Correct)

    As mentioned above, the primary carbocation rearranges via a hydride shift to generate the more stable isopropyl carbocation ($$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}^+\text{CH}_3$$) intermediate.

  • Statement C: Multiple substitution is inevitable (Correct)

    The alkyl group introduced onto the benzene ring is an electron-donating group (via inductive and hyperconjugation effects). This activates the benzene ring, making the product more reactive toward electrophilic substitution than the starting benzene itself. Consequently, polyalkylation (multiple substitutions) is a major drawback and is highly favored.

  • Statement D: Introducing electron-donating substituent on benzene will not produce any alkyl benzene (Incorrect)

    Electron-donating groups activate the benzene ring towards electrophilic aromatic substitution, making Friedel-Crafts alkylation happen even more readily. (It is strong electron-withdrawing groups, like $$-\text{NO}_2$$, that deactivate the ring and stop the reaction).

Correct Option: B and C only

  • Mechanism: This is the Carbylamine reaction (Hofmann's isocyanide test). The primary amine reacts with chloroform in a basic medium via a dichlorocarbene ($$:\text{CCl}_2$$) intermediate to form an isocyanide.
  • Product: Benzyl isocyanide ($$\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{NC}$$)

  • Mechanism: Potassium cyanide ($$\text{KCN}$$) is ionic, providing free $$\text{CN}^-$$ ions where the negatively charged carbon acts as the nucleophile. Furthermore, the starting alkyl chain already has two carbon atoms instead of one.

B. Anomers of glucose differ in configuration at C-1 in cyclic hemiacetal structure.

C. Melting point of $$\alpha$$-anomer of glucose is greater than $$\beta$$-anomer.

D. Specific rotation of $$\alpha$$-anomer is +19° while for $$\beta$$-anomer is +112°.

E. $$\alpha$$ and $$\beta$$-anomers of glucose are prepared by crystallization of saturated glucose solution at 303 K and 371 K respectively.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

explanations.title: method2
explanations.content:
Glucose exists predominantly in cyclic hemiacetal forms and hence exists as two anomers, namely $$\alpha$$- and $$\beta$$-glucose. Therefore, statement A is correct.

The two anomers differ only in the configuration at the anomeric carbon, i.e., C-1 in the cyclic hemiacetal structure. Therefore, statement B is correct.

The melting point of $$\alpha$$-D-glucose is $$419\ \text{K}$$, whereas that of $$\beta$$-D-glucose is $$423\ \text{K}$$. Hence, the melting point of the $$\alpha$$-anomer is not greater than that of the $$\beta$$-anomer. Therefore, statement C is incorrect.

The specific rotation of pure $$\alpha$$-D-glucose is $$+112^\circ$$, while that of pure $$\beta$$-D-glucose is $$+19^\circ$$. Thus, the values given in statement D are interchanged. Therefore, statement D is incorrect.

The $$\alpha$$-anomer is obtained by crystallization of a saturated glucose solution at $$303\ \text{K}$$, whereas the $$\beta$$-anomer is obtained by crystallization at $$371\ \text{K}$$. Therefore, statement E is correct.

Hence, the correct statements are A, B and E.

explanations.title: method3
explanations.content:
Statement A: Glucose exists in two anomeric forms.

This statement is correct. Glucose exists in two different crystalline forms, which are named as the $\alpha$-form and the $\beta$-form. These are known as anomers.

Statement B: Anomers of glucose differ in configuration at $\mathrm{C}-1$ in cyclic hemiacetal structure.

This statement is correct. The $\alpha$ and $\beta$ forms of glucose are cyclic hemiacetals that differ only in the spatial arrangement of the hydroxyl group (-OH) at the first carbon atom ($\mathrm{C}-1$). This specific carbon is referred to as the anomeric carbon.

Statement C: Melting point of $\alpha$ - anomer of glucose is greater than $\beta$ - anomer.

This statement is incorrect. According to experimental data, the melting point of the $\alpha$-form of glucose is $419 \text{ K}$, whereas the melting point of the $\beta$-form is slightly higher, at $423 \text{ K}$. Therefore, the melting point of the $\beta$-anomer is greater than that of the $\alpha$-anomer.

Statement D: Specific rotation of $\alpha$ - anomer is $+19^{\circ}$ while for $\beta$ - anomer is $+112^{\circ}$

This statement is incorrect because the values are interchanged. The specific rotation of the pure $\alpha$-anomer is $+112.2^{\circ}$, and the specific rotation of the pure $\beta$-anomer is $+19.2^{\circ}$. Over time, both undergo mutarotation to reach an equilibrium specific rotation of $+52.5^{\circ}$.

Statement E: $\alpha$ and $\beta$ - anomers of glucose are prepared by crystallization of saturated glucose solution at 303 K and 371 K respectively.

This statement is correct. The $\alpha$-form is typically obtained by the crystallization from a concentrated aqueous solution of glucose at room temperature, around $303 \text{ K}$. On the other hand, the $\beta$-form is obtained by crystallizing it from a hot and saturated aqueous solution at $371 \text{ K}$.

From the analysis above, the mathematically and factually correct statements are A, B, and E.

Therefore, the correct choice is Option D.

question_text:
Given below are two statements:
Statement I: Sodium dichromate and potassium dichromate are classified as primary standards in titrimetric analysis.
Statement II: Phenolphthalein is a weak base, therefore it dissociates in acidic medium.
In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below

options.A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
options.B: Both Statement I and Statement II are false
options.C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false
options.D: Statement I is false but Statement II is true

explanations.title: method2
explanations.content:
Statement I: Sodium dichromate and potassium dichromate are classified as primary standards in titrimetric analysis.

Incorrect, Only Potassium dichromate is classified as primary standards in titrimetric analysis as it is more stable and pure. Unlike, Sodium dichromate, it is highly hygroscopic (readily absorbs moisture from the air) which prevents Sodium dichromate from maintaining its original mass and purity.

Statement II: Phenolphthalein is a weak base, therefore it dissociates in acidic medium.

Incorrect, Phenolphthalein is a weak acid, not a weak base. It is largely unionized in acidic medium and gets ionized in basic medium (by showing pink colour).

explanations.title: method3
explanations.content:
Analysis of Statement I :

In titrimetric analysis, a primary standard is a substance of high purity that is stable and not hygroscopic, meaning its exact mass can be weighed directly to prepare a standard solution. According to NCERT, potassium dichromate ($K_2Cr_2O_7$) is stable and non-hygroscopic, making it a good primary standard.

However, sodium dichromate ($Na_2Cr_2O_7$) is highly hygroscopic (deliquescent). It readily absorbs moisture from the atmosphere, which changes its mass continuously. Due to this property, it cannot be weighed accurately to prepare a standard solution. Therefore, sodium dichromate is not classified as a primary standard.

Because of the incorrect claim about sodium dichromate, Statement I is false.

Analysis of Statement II :

Phenolphthalein is an indicator widely used in acid-base titrations. Chemically, it is a weak organic acid, not a weak base. We often represent it as $HPh$.

Since phenolphthalein is a weak acid, its dissociation is governed by the following equilibrium:

$$HPh \rightleftharpoons H^+ + Ph^-$$

In an acidic medium, there is already an excess of hydrogen ions ($H^+$). According to Le Chatelier's principle (specifically the common ion effect), the high concentration of $H^+$ suppresses the dissociation of the weak acid $HPh$, causing it to remain mostly in its undissociated, colourless form. It is in a basic medium that phenolphthalein actually dissociates to form the pink-coloured $Ph^-$ ion.

Because phenolphthalein is a weak acid and does not dissociate significantly in an acidic medium, Statement II is false.

Conclusion :

Since both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect, the correct option is Option B.

Correct Answer :

Option B: Both Statement I and Statement II are false

$$BrF_5$$, $$XeF_5^-$$, $$BF_4^-$$, $$ICl_4^-$$, $$XeF_4$$, $$SF_4$$, $$NH_4^+$$, $$ClF_3$$, $$XeF_2$$, $$ICl_2^-$$
Number of species having $$sp^3d$$ hybridized central atom is _______.

explanations.title: method2
explanations.content:
The hybridization of a central atom can be determined using the Steric Number (SN) formula:

$$(\text{SN}=\frac{1}{2}\left[V+M-C+A\right])$$

Where 

$$V = \text{valence electrons of central atom}$$, 

$$M = \text{monovalent atoms}$$, 

$$C = \text{cationic charge}$$, and 

$$A = \text{anionic charge}$$. 

A steric number of 5 corresponds to $$(sp^{3}d)$$ hybridization.

1. Species with $$(sp^{3}d)$$ Hybridization $$(\text{SN} = 5)$$:

  • $$(\text{SF}_{4}):$$ $$(\text{SN} = \frac{1}{2}(6 + 4) = 5)$$ $$(\rightarrow )$$ 4 Bond Pairs + 1 Lone Pair (See-saw shape)
  • $$(\text{ClF}_{3}):$$ $$(\text{SN} = \frac{1}{2}(7 + 3) = 5)$$ $$(\rightarrow )$$ 3 Bond Pairs + 2 Lone Pairs (T-shape)
  • $$(\text{XeF}_{2}):$$ $$(\text{SN} = \frac{1}{2}(8 + 2) = 5)$$ $$(\rightarrow )$$ 2 Bond Pairs + 3 Lone Pairs (Linear shape)
  • $$(\text{ICl}_{2}^{-}):$$ $$(\text{SN} = \frac{1}{2}(7 + 2 + 1) = 5)$$ $$(\rightarrow )$$ 2 Bond Pairs + 3 Lone Pairs (Linear shape)

2. Other Species in the List:

  • $$(\text{BrF}_{5}):$$ $$(\text{SN} = \frac{1}{2}(7 + 5) = 6 \rightarrow sp^3d^2)$$ (Square pyramidal)
  • $$(\text{XeF}_{5}^{-}):$$ $$(\text{SN} = \frac{1}{2}(8 + 5 + 1) = 7 \rightarrow sp^3d^3)$$ (Pentagonal planar)
  • $$(\text{BF}_{4}^{-}):$$ $$(\text{SN} = \frac{1}{2}(3 + 4 + 1) = 4 \rightarrow sp^3)$$ (Tetrahedral)
  • $$(\text{ICl}_{4}^{-}):$$ $$(\text{SN} = \frac{1}{2}(7 + 4 + 1) = 6 \rightarrow sp^3d^2)$$ (Square planar)
  • $$(\text{XeF}_{4}):$$ $$(\text{SN} = \frac{1}{2}(8 + 4) = 6 \rightarrow sp^3d^2)$$ (Square planar)
  • $$(\text{NH}_{4}^{+}):$$ $$(\text{SN} = \frac{1}{2}(5 + 4 - 1) = 4 \rightarrow sp^3)$$ (Tetrahedral)

Species having $$sp^3{}d$$ hybridization are:

$$SF_4,\ ClF_3,\ XeF_2,\ ICl_2^-$$

Total number: 4

question_text: In an estimation of sulphur by Carius method 0.2 g of the substance gave 0.6 g of BaSO$$_4$$. The percentage of sulphur in the substance is _______%. (Given molar mass in g mol$$^{-1}$$ S: 32, BaSO$$_4$$: 231)

explanations.title: method2
explanations.content:
In Carius method, the Sulphur $$(S)$$ is converted into Barium Sulphate $$(BaSO_{4})$$.

Given:

  • Mass of substance $$= 0.2 g$$
  • Mass of $$BaSO_{4}$$ formed $$= 0.6 g$$
  • Molar mass of $$BaSO_{4}$$ $$=231$$
  • Atomic mass of $$S = 32$$

Mass of sulphur in $$0.6 g$$ of $$BaSO_{4}$$​:

$$Mass\ of\ S=\frac{32}{231}\times\ 0.6=0.0831g$$

Percentage of Sulphur:

$$\ \%\ S=\frac{0.0831g}{0.2}\times\ 100$$

$$\ \%\ S=41.56\ \%\ $$

The percentage of sulphur in the substance is 41.56%

explanations.title: method3
explanations.content:
Given:

  • Mass of the substance = $ 0.2 \, \text{g} $

  • Mass of $ \mathrm{BaSO_4} $ formed = $ 0.6 \, \text{g} $

  • Molar mass of $ \mathrm{BaSO_4} = 231 \, \text{g mol}^{-1} $

  • Molar mass of S = $ 32 \, \text{g mol}^{-1} $

$ \text{Moles of } \mathrm{BaSO_4} = \frac{\text{Mass}}{\text{Molar mass}} = \frac{0.6}{231} $

$ \text{Moles of } \mathrm{BaSO_4} = 0.002597 \, \text{mol} $

In one mole of $ \mathrm{BaSO_4} $, there is one mole of sulphur.

Hence,

$ \text{Moles of sulphur} = \text{Moles of } \mathrm{BaSO_4} = 0.002597 \, \text{mol} $

$ \text{Mass of S} = \text{Moles} \times \text{Atomic mass} = 0.002597 \times 32 $

$ \text{Mass of S} = 0.0831 \, \text{g} $

$ \%\ \text{of S} = \frac{\text{Mass of S}}{\text{Mass of sample}} \times 100 $

$ \%\ \text{of S} = \frac{0.0831}{0.2} \times 100 = 41.55\% $

$ \boxed{\text{Percentage of sulphur in the substance} = 41.55\%} $

question_text: One mole of phenol is treated with dilute HNO$$_3$$ at 298 K to give a mixture of products. The mixture is separated by steam distillation. The steam volatile compound (X) is separated. The increase in percentage of oxygen in (X) with respect to phenol is _______ $$\times 10^{-1}$$ %. (Given molar mass in g mol$$^{-1}$$ H:1, C:12, N:14, O:16)

explanations.title: method2
explanations.content:
Step 1: Identify Compound (X)

  • When phenol is treated with dilute $$HNO_3$$ at $$298 K$$, it undergoes nitration to give a mixture of o-nitrophenol and p-nitrophenol.
  • On steam distillation, o-nitrophenol is separated because it is steam volatile due to intramolecular hydrogen bonding. 
  • Therefore, compound (X) is o-nitrophenol. 

Step 2: Oxygen Percentage in Phenol ($$C_{6}H_{5}OH$$)

Molar Mass: $$6(12)+5(1)+1(16)+1=94$$

Percentage of Oxygen :

$$\frac{16}{94}\times\ 100=17.02\ \%\ $$

Step 3: Oxygen Percentage in o-nitrophenol ($$C_{6}H_{5}NO_3$$)

Molar Mass: $$6(12)+5(1)+14+3(16)=139$$

Percentage of Oxygen:$$\frac{48}{139}\times\ 100=34.53\ \%\ $$

Step 4: Increase in Oxygen Percentage

$$34.53\ -17.02=17.51$$

so,

$$17.51\ \%\ =175.1\times\ 10^{-1}\ \%\ $$

Therefore,

The increase in percentage of oxygen in (X) with respect to phenol is 175 $$\times 10^{-1}$$ %.

explanations.title: method3
explanations.content:
Step 1: Calculate the percentage of oxygen in phenol.

The molecular formula of phenol is $ \mathrm{C_6H_6O} $. Its molecular mass is:

$$ (6 \times 12) + (6 \times 1) + 16 = 94~\mathrm{g/mol} $$

Percentage of oxygen in phenol:

$$ \frac{16}{94} \times 100 = 17.02\% $$

Step 2: Calculate the percentage of oxygen in o-nitrophenol.

When phenol reacts with dilute $ \mathrm{HNO_3} $, the steam-volatile product formed is o-nitrophenol ($ \mathrm{C_6H_5NO_3} $).

Molecular mass of o-nitrophenol:

$$ (6 \times 12) + (5 \times 1) + 14 + (3 \times 16) = 139~\mathrm{g/mol} $$

Percentage of oxygen in o-nitrophenol:

$$ \frac{48}{139} \times 100 = 34.53\% $$

Step 3: Find the percentage increase in oxygen.

Increase in oxygen percentage:

$$ 34.53 - 17.02 = 17.5 $$

Step 4: Express the answer in the required form.

The increase in percentage of oxygen with respect to phenol is:

$$ 17.5 \times 10^{-1} = 175 $$

$$A(g) \rightleftharpoons B(g) + C(g)$$


The magnitude of $$\frac{\Delta H^\circ}{R}$$ calculated from the above data is _______. (Nearest integer)

explanations.title: method2
explanations.content:
To find the magnitude of $$\ \frac{\triangle\ H^{\circ\ }}{R}$$, we use the integrated form of the van 't Hoff equation:

$$\log_{10}K_p=-\frac{\triangle H^{\circ\ }}{2.303RT}\ +$$ Constant

Step 1: Identify the slope

The equation is in the form of $$y=mx+c$$, 

where:

$$y=\log_{10}K_p$$

$$x=\frac{1}{T}$$

$$m\left(slope\right)=-\frac{\triangle H^{\circ\ }}{2.303R}\ $$

Using the first two points from the table:

$$\left(x_1,y_1\right)=\left(0.05,3.5\right)$$

$$\left(x_2,y_2\right)=\left(0.06,2.5\right)$$

Therefore, 

$$slope\left(m\right)=\frac{y_2-y_1}{x_2-x_1}=\frac{2.5-3.5}{0.06-0.05}=-\frac{0.1}{0.01}=-100$$

Step 2: Calculate $$\ \frac{\triangle\ H^{\circ\ }}{R}$$

Equating the calculated slop $$(m)$$

$$-100=-\frac{\triangle H^{\circ\ }}{2.303R}$$

$$100\times\ 2.303=\frac{\triangle H^{\circ\ }}{R}$$

$$230.3=\frac{\triangle H^{\circ\ }}{R}$$

Therefore, the nearest integer is 230.

explanations.title: method3
explanations.content:
For the relation between equilibrium constant and temperature, we use the integrated vanât Hoff equation:

$$ \log_{10} K_p = -\frac{\Delta H^\circ}{2.303R}\cdot \frac{1}{T} + \text{constant} $$

This is in the form of a straight line:

$$ y = mx + c $$

where

  • $y = \log_{10} K_p$

  • $x = \dfrac{1}{T}$

  • slope $m = -\dfrac{\Delta H^\circ}{2.303R}$

Now calculate the slope from the given data.

Using points $(0.05, 3.5)$ and $(0.06, 2.5)$:

$$ m = \frac{2.5 - 3.5}{0.06 - 0.05} = \frac{-1}{0.01} = -100 $$

So,

$$ -\frac{\Delta H^\circ}{2.303R} = -100 $$

Hence,

$$ \frac{\Delta H^\circ}{R} = 100 \times 2.303 $$

$$ \frac{\Delta H^\circ}{R} = 230.3 $$

Therefore, the magnitude of $\dfrac{\Delta H^\circ}{R}$ is

$$ \boxed{230} $$

Nearest integer: $\boxed{230}$

question_text: If the half life of a first order reaction is 6.93 minutes then the time required for completion of 99% of the reaction will be _______ minutes. (Given: log 2 = 0.3010)

explanations.title: method2
explanations.content:
Step 1: Calculate the rate constant $$(k)$$.

For, first order reaction the rate constant $$(k)$$ is related to $$t_{1/2}$$ by this formula:

$$t_{1/2}=\frac{0.693}{k}$$

since, 

$$t_{1/2}=6.93$$

$$k=\frac{0.693}{6.93}=0.1\ \min^{-1}$$

Step 2: Calculate time for 99% Completion

The integrated rate law for a first-order reaction give us to solve for time $$(t)$$:

$$t=\frac{2.303}{k\ }\log\left(\frac{\left[A_o\right]}{\left[A_t\right]}\right)$$

For 99% completion, 1% of the reactant remains.

Let's assume the initial concentration $$[A]_0 = 100$$, then the final concentration $$[A]_t = 1$$:

$$t=\frac{2.303}{0.1}\log\left(\frac{100}{1}\right)$$

$$t=\frac{2.303}{0.1}\times\ 2$$

$$t=23.03\times\ 2$$

$$t=46.06$$ minutes

Therefore, the time required for completion of 99% of the reaction will be 46.06 minutes.

explanations.title: method3
explanations.content:
For a first order reaction,

$$ t_{1/2}=\frac{0.693}{k} $$

Given:

$$ t_{1/2}=6.93 \text{ min} $$

So,

$$ k=\frac{0.693}{6.93}=0.1\ \text{min}^{-1} $$

Now, $99\%$ completion means only $1\%$ of the reactant is left.

So,

$$ \frac{[A]_0}{[A]}=\frac{100}{1}=100 $$

For a first order reaction,

$$ t=\frac{2.303}{k}\log\frac{[A]_0}{[A]} $$

Substituting the values:

$$ t=\frac{2.303}{0.1}\log 100 $$

Since,

$$ \log 100=2 $$

therefore,

$$ t=\frac{2.303}{0.1}\times 2 $$

$$ t=23.03\times 2=46.06 \text{ min} $$

Hence, the time required for $99\%$ completion of the reaction is

$$ \boxed{46.06\ \text{minutes}} $$
